1:
Where this chapter stands is noticed first. Gill places it in the first year of Belshazzar, seventeen years before the fall of the monarchy already related. Henry observes that the king's name is spelt differently here, the earlier form meaning that Bel treasures up riches and this one that Bel is on fire by the enemy, the god of the Chaldeans having prospered and being now about to be consumed. Ellicott quotes Jerome, that the earlier chapters follow the order of history while here are narrated dreams seen at particular times, of which the prophet alone was conscious, carrying no weight of sign among the heathen nations and written only that the memory of them might survive. He adds that the phrase about the sum of the matters shows Daniel had other visions at this time.

Why the vision was given at all is answered the same way by three of them. Calvin says the prophets had all held out the hope of deliverance, so that one would suppose the Church was promised a wholly peaceful state after the return, whereas history testifies how differently it turned out; the faithful must have fallen away had they not been warned of the disturbances at hand. Henry puts it as the correction of a mistake, that the Jews, misunderstanding certain prophecies, flattered themselves with hopes of uninterrupted tranquillity after their return, and are told they shall have tribulation instead; Wesley says the visions were recorded to rectify that very error. Calvin adds that the prophet's office changes here, since God had appointed him an interpreter to profane kings and now appoints him a teacher within the Church.

What the great sea is has to be settled. Clarke takes it of the Mediterranean, so called to distinguish it from the lakes the Hebrews also called seas. Keil and Delitzsch denies this outright, since such a geographical reference is foreign to the context: because the beasts represent forms of the world-power, the sea must represent that out of which they arise, the whole heathen world. Ellicott agrees, granting that the phrase generally means the Mediterranean but holding that the interpretation given later justifies taking the sea for the nations. Calvin does not name the water but explains the storm, that on solid ground such concussion is seldom felt as at sea, and that four winds are named to show the commotion would come from every quarter at once.

Calvin also says how bitter the vision must have been. The faithful were counting the years Jeremiah had prescribed, the seventieth was at hand, and God had promised an end of their troubles; and now they are told to prepare for the fiercest winds, so that they might well have suspected God of not performing his promises. Henry adds that Daniel both wrote the dream and told its sum to his brethren, to intimate that the church is taught by scripture and by preaching alike.

Why kingdoms appear as beasts is explained from what they do. Gill says they are called beasts for the rapine and cruelty by which they were obtained, and great ones because they consisted of many kingdoms, like beasts of enormous size. Calvin grants that empires in themselves are beautiful reflections of divine wisdom when conducted by the law of equity, but says few who obtain supreme sway acknowledge themselves divinely created for the office, and that since the greatest kingdoms are the greatest robberies, as was once said to Alexander, the vice belongs to the rulers and not to the ordinance of God. Ellicott notes that the figures imply monstrous form rather than size, and that the beasts rise in succession; Clarke lists their differences in people, laws and administration. Keil and Delitzsch observes that winged symbolic figures found at Babylon have been used as evidence that the book was composed there and as explaining its Babylonian colouring.
4:
Gill takes the lion for the Babylonian power, named for its strength and majesty and answering to the head of gold. Clarke reports from Newton that these are monstrous productions but that such emblems were usual among the eastern nations, a winged lion being visible in the ruins of Persepolis, and horns being given in hieroglyphic writing to beasts which have none. He adds a conjecture of his own, that heraldry arose from what was gathered out of such symbols and from the little then known of the Egyptian hieroglyphics, which is why we have griffins and unicorns and two-headed swans. Ellicott takes lion and eagle as emblems of strength and swiftness, and says the plucking of the wings leaves the beast without its unrestrained motion, the raising of it into a man's posture answering to the man's heart given it. He is careful not to fix the reference: there is not sufficient historical detail about the last years of that reign, and though Jerome suggested the king's madness and recovery, the subject of the vision is the kingdom rather than the king.

Calvin reads the order of the beasts as a descent. Some superiority is granted to the lion because the world is always growing worse; Cyrus was a prudent prince and yet never reached the temperance of former ages, and Isaiah says of the Persians that they desire neither silver nor gold but thirst after human blood. A bear, Calvin continues, is a mean and foul animal, slothful as well as cruel, and displeasing beside the lion; and the Persians were not civilised like the Chaldeans but lay hid like wild beasts among their mountains. Clarke gives plainer reasons, that the largest bears were found in Media and the animal was called all-devouring by Aristotle, while the Persians were notorious for the cruelty of their punishments.

What it means that the bear raised itself on one side is unsettled. Keil and Delitzsch rejects the rabbinic rendering that it established a dominion, since the numeral will not bear it and the character of a single compact dominion belongs to the second kingdom in no case. Ellicott makes the two sides answer to the two arms of the image, so that the raising of one shows the Persian element surpassing the Median; Calvin takes it instead of the obscure origin of the kingdom, the fame of the Persians being shut within their mountains until Cyrus won them a name. The three ribs are counted as variously: Clarke offers a beast that has just fed, or three curved tusks, or three throats by which the three empires were absorbed; Ellicott takes them for kingdoms already swallowed, named since Hippolytus as the Babylonians, Lydians and Egyptians; Wesley makes them Babylonian subjects who had revolted.

The third beast is agreed to be the Greek power. Ellicott prefers panther to leopard, and notes that unity marks the first beast, duality the second and quadruplicity the third. Keil and Delitzsch says the panther is neither so kingly as the lion nor so strong as the bear but surpasses both in springing agility, so that its subordination repeats the gradation already marked in the metals. Clarke gives three reasons for the emblem, swiftness, the spots answering to the many nations of the empire and to Alexander's own character, and the leopard's willingness to attack a lion though smaller; he counts four wings against the earlier two because nothing equalled a conquest from the Adriatic to the Ganges in twelve years, and takes the four heads of the generals who divided the empire. Calvin distrusts the accumulated points of likeness, thinks it enough that the third empire is meant, and turns to the man: Alexander excelled in no virtue, mere rashness seized upon him, and even had he never tasted wine his ambition would have intoxicated him, so that his whole life was drunken.
7:
The fourth beast is agreed to be Rome, and everything else about it is disputed. Gill rejects the Turkish empire and the kingdom of the Seleucidae alike, since neither the characters nor the duration agree; Clarke says the Roman reading is allowed on all hands, and dates the reduction of Macedon, Pergamos, Syria and Egypt into provinces to show how it might be said to devour the whole earth. Calvin agrees so far, but reports that those who confess it disagree at once, many transferring what follows to the Pope and others holding that the Turkish kingdom is comprehended under the Roman; the Jews mostly take the second course of necessity, he says, since it is clear from this prediction that Christ's kingdom was erected by the overthrow of the Roman dominion, and, not finding their Christ, they join the later monarchy to the earlier.

Why no animal is named at all is noticed by three of them. Calvin says the beast is given no fixed name because nothing like it ever existed, and that by adding no similitude the prophet signifies how horrible the monster was, no animal in the world being fierce enough to represent it. He contrasts the previous empire, whose conqueror was content with fame and granted liberty to all who flattered him, with a power that held Asia Minor, Syria, Greece, Macedon, both the Spains, Gaul and part of Germany, and at length Britain. Keil and Delitzsch makes the same point, that its terribleness and the absence of any beast it can be likened to mark it off from all before it. Ellicott says it is so terrible that Daniel can hardly find words, and notes that the ten horns answer to the ten toes of the image.

Calvin then sets a limit that the others do not. Interpreters begin to vary here, he says, some twisting the little horn to mean the Pope and others the Turk, and neither seems to him probable; both are wrong because they suppose the whole course of Christ's kingdom is described, whereas God wished only to declare what should happen up to the first advent. That, he says, is the error of all who try to embrace under this vision the perpetual state of the Church to the end of the world. The vision was given because the minds of the pious would fail them in the convulsions then at hand, so the prophet does not proceed beyond the promised redemption; and on that reckoning the little horn is Julius Caesar and the Caesars who followed.

The other identifications are set out plainly. Clarke reports that among Protestant writers the little horn is considered the popedom, and names the three uprooted horns as the exarchate of Ravenna, the kingdom of the Lombards and the state of Rome, with the dates at which each was made over; he also passes on the alternative of Calmet, that ten Syrian kings are meant, and lists them from the first Seleucus onward. Wesley leaves it open between the Turk and the Roman antichrist.

The eyes and the mouth are read as marking a person. Keil and Delitzsch takes eyes and seeing as symbols of insight, so that this king excels the others in prudence, and then asks why the eyes should be those of a man, since the horn is already shown to signify a man by having eyes and speech at all. Ellicott answers that a man is intended rather than a kingdom, though the man may represent one, the eyes indicating craft and cunning and the mouth speaking great things implying vain-glory. Calvin draws attention to the prophet's own attention, that he considered the horns by a heavenly impulse, so that it is our duty not to read carelessly but to weigh what the Spirit intends here.
9:
Whether the thrones are thrown down or set up turns on one word. Gill reports that Jewish interpreters take it of the thrones of the four monarchies demolished, while the old versions render it that the thrones were set up for judges to sit on; Wesley keeps the first sense, that the kingdoms of this world were destroyed by the eternal king. Clarke argues for the first from usage elsewhere in the book, where the word can be used in no other sense than throwing down, and adds that the reference is to preparations for a general assize, the president sitting with his assessors on either side in a semicircle. Henry allows that set up may as well be read, and reports a rabbinic admission that two thrones are meant. Calvin inclines to the second sense, since the prophet at once represents myriads of angels standing before God, which suits assessors rather than deposed kings; but he says the readings differ little in substance. Keil and Delitzsch renders it that the seats were thrown, meaning placed in order quickly.

Who occupies the other seats is disputed on the same evidence. Keil and Delitzsch takes them for angels, rejecting both the rabbinic view that they are the elders of Israel and the view that they are glorified men, and distinguishes them from the thousands named next; Calvin agrees, since angels are often described as assessors of the Deity. Ellicott grants that the seats have been interpreted of angels, but holds that a truer explanation lies in the promise made to the apostles.

Ellicott then answers an argument about the title itself. Granting that the word for the Ancient is elsewhere applied to a Babylonian deity, he holds that the titles given to that deity, generator and father of the gods, are so at variance with Old Testament doctrine that it is inconceivable Daniel took any part of his vision from Babylonian mythology; and he says the same of a parallel drawn between another such figure and the Son of man. He takes the age as expressing the majesty of the judge and the wheels as representing divine omnipresence. Clarke observes that this is the only place in the sacred writings where God the Father is represented in a human form.

Whether the scene is the last judgment divides them sharply. Clarke says it is not spoken of the final judgment at all but of the judgment executed on the fourth beast and on the horn, which must fall when the beast falls. Calvin says the appearance of God as judge is what led many to extend the prophecy to the second advent, an interpretation he calls by no means correct. Henry allows all three at once: that the scene proclaims God's righteous government of the world by providence, that it may point at the destruction brought on the empire that tyrannised over his people, but that it seems principally designed to describe the last judgment, which, though it may be many ages off, was set here so that the people of God in every age might encourage themselves under their troubles.

The attendants and the books close the scene. Calvin says the numbers are not to be reckoned but signify forces at hand far surpassing any armies the most powerful princes collect, and that angels were created to execute his commands, being as it were his hands in heaven and earth, always present and needing no muster. Gill reads the river of fire as the copious judgments of God, the full flow of his wrath, which cannot be stopped; Calvin adds that God always shows something terrible when he appears to his servants, not merely to astonish but to excite reverence, since we never sufficiently comprehend his majesty except when humbled. Ellicott glosses the books as the unerring record of man's thoughts and deeds, written in the unfailing memory of God.
11:
What brings on the sentence is the speech. Gill says that from the moment the blasphemous words were heard the prophet kept looking to see the issue, concluding that such intolerable things must be noticed in a way of correction, especially now that the Judge had appeared with everything prepared for a judicial process. Ellicott makes the blasphemy the express cause of the judgment, and notices something unexpected: one would have looked for the crowning scene to be the uprooting of the little horn, whereas it is the fourth monster itself that is slain and burned, the blaspheming spirit having issued from it. He takes the burning flame as the doctrine of final retribution so far as it is revealed here.

Clarke draws a distinction between this destruction and the others. He passes on the remark of Newton that when dominion was taken from the earlier beasts their bodies were suffered to continue in being, whereas when dominion is taken from this one the body is totally destroyed, because other kingdoms succeeded to those but none is to succeed to this. Wesley says shortly that the passage cannot but mean the ruin and judgment of antichrist.

Calvin refers the slaying of the beast to the end of the Roman power and argues the point from history. From the time foreigners obtained the mastery, he says, the fourth beast ceased to flourish, the name being retained in mockery of the ancient monarchy; when Spaniards and Africans acquired the absolute sway, it would be foolish to go on calling Rome the mistress of the world. In his own day the Germans said they possessed the Roman empire, but while the title had passed to them Rome itself was in servitude. After Nero, he observes, scarcely a single Roman obtained the empire, and God branded it with the most disgraceful ignominy when a swineherd was made emperor by the lust of the soldiery, the senate keeping its name but obliged to ratify whatever man the soldiers chose. On that reckoning the presumptuous speaking came to an end shortly after the promulgation of the gospel, the destruction of the beast following upon the light which the preaching of the gospel shed on the world.

The fate of the other three is added as an afterthought, and its grammar is disputed. Keil and Delitzsch says the construction forbids making the first clause depend on the sentence before it, and denies that the other beasts can mean kingdoms of the fourth monarchy left standing after the horn had done its work, since with the death of the beast the whole fourth monarchy is destroyed. Calvin holds that the verbs should be pluperfects, the power having already been removed from the other three before the fourth was slain, and explains the disorder by the habit of the Hebrew writers, who repeat afterwards whatever has been omitted and do not always observe the order of time. Ellicott states the substance plainly, that the dominions of the first three had passed away while their lives were prolonged up to the definite point that seemed fit to God and no further.

The measured time at the end is where Calvin dwells. He observes that two different words are used which signify the same thing, and takes the whole to teach that nothing happens accidentally but that all things are carried on in their own season as God has decreed them in heaven. He suggests that the phrase may point to the protracted length of these afflictions, since they were not to pass away suddenly like clouds; not only severe but lengthened trials await the faithful, and these must weary them unless the hope of a better issue props them up. What the words promise is that God would at length deliver his Church when he had exercised its patience, since a length of time has its own limits.
13:
The turn to a second scene is marked before the figure is identified. Keil and Delitzsch observes that the judgment does not end with the destruction of the world-power, which is only the first act, immediately followed by the second, the erection of the kingdom of God by the Son of man; and that he who comes is not named but only described as resembling a man, surrounded by clouds. Gill notes that the fresh preface and the word behold mark the object as new, and Calvin says the repetition shows the prophet's alertness when God shows himself present.

The word like is where the interest lies. Ellicott argues that the title implies one descended from man, but that since the person is only like one of human descent it follows that he was not merely a man; and he holds that the early Jewish and Christian readings which take this of the Messiah are confirmed by the Saviour's own use of the title. Clarke says the words most certainly point out the Lord Jesus, the son of miserable man, who took our nature upon him to redeem us, and that he applied them to himself before the high priests in order to prove himself the Messiah. Calvin resolves the same word differently. He notes that it might be twisted to favour the folly of the Manichees, who thought Christ's body only imaginary and who wrest in the same way the words of Paul about his being found in the likeness of men; but Paul is speaking there of his state and not of the essence of his human nature, and here the reason is different, since Christ had not yet taken our flesh. He began to be man, on Calvin's account, when he appeared as Mediator, not having assumed the seed of Abraham before he was joined to us; had he put on human flesh from the beginning he would not have been the Messiah promised under the Law as the son of Abraham and of David.

The coming to the Ancient of days is read as an investiture. Wesley takes the clouds as marking a coming glorious, swift and terrible, and refers the approach to the ascension, when Christ received his royal investiture for the protection of his church. Calvin uses the same clause against an objection: some argue from it that Christ cannot be true and eternal God, since he comes to the Ancient of days; but the words are spoken of the person of the Mediator, and all doubt is removed when the prophet adds that dominion was given him, for it was given him as Mediator, as God manifest in flesh. Power was given, he adds, to inform us how God reigns by means of his hand: if we had to seek God without a Mediator his distance would be far too great, whereas when a Mediator offers himself in our own nature the nearness is such that faith easily passes beyond the world.

How far the promise reaches is again a question of limits. Calvin insists that the giving of the kingdom is properly to be understood of the commencement of Christ's reign and not of its final close, as many interpreters force the passage, while granting that what is narrated here is not yet complete. Clarke takes the everlasting dominion to mean that Christianity shall increase and prevail to the end of the world, and notes that our Lord applied the words to himself after his resurrection. Gill allows that Christ had a kingdom before this, and takes the promise of one more extensive, to be fulfilled when the kingdoms of this world become his. Ellicott adds a small but weighty grammatical point, that in this dialect the word rendered serve is used only of rendering divine service or worship, so that the Son of man is here spoken of as God.
15:
One word in the description of the prophet's distress carries a good deal of weight. Gill and Ellicott note that the term means a sheath, the soul being in the body as a sword in its scabbard, and Henry adds that the body is then no more to the soul than a scabbard to the weapon. Clarke draws three inferences from the same noun: that the human spirit is different from the body, that it has a proper subsistence independent of it, the body being only its sheath for a time, and that it may exist apart from the body as the sword does from its sheath.

Why the vision should have overwhelmed him is variously explained. Henry says the manner of the discovery put his thoughts so much to the stretch that his spirits failed, until by degrees he recollected himself and set the comforts of the vision against its terrors. Calvin makes the fainting instructive: if a prophet so remarkable felt his spirit nearly vanish away, those who have scarcely tasted these mysteries can reach no such height unless they shake off all human sensations. He also distinguishes this from ordinary alarm: no one faints without a cause, and Daniel is careful to say he was troubled by the mystery itself.

That he asked for an explanation is taken as an example. Henry says those who would know the full sense of what they hear from God must ask by fervent prayer and diligent search. Calvin notes his modesty in flying to an instructor because he was conscious of his ignorance, and draws the rule that we are not to reject visions but to seek their interpretation from God; and though angels no longer descend, yet since Scripture is obscure to us we should not reject whatever surpasses our capacity but use the remedy Daniel used. Wesley identifies the one addressed as a ministering angel. Keil and Delitzsch notes that the verb is subjunctive rather than past, and that the one standing by is from among those about the throne, so that the vision was still going on.

Whether kings or kingdoms are meant is settled quickly. Gill reports that the versions and the Jewish interpreters render it kingdoms, and Ellicott that kingdoms are frequently represented by their heads or founders, so that the two words are used synonymously. Keil and Delitzsch says four kingdoms are meant, and reports that one critic argued from the future tense that the first kingdom was still to come, and therefore could not be the Babylonian, since the vision fell under Belshazzar. Calvin meets the difficulty by asking what the angel was doing rather than what the tense requires: the Chaldean power had long since arisen, but the purpose was to teach a people who saw themselves as good as buried, exile being to them equivalent to the tomb, that revolutions need not disturb them.

The saints who receive the kingdom are described and the phrase disputed. Gill reads the words as the saints of the most high Ones, or else of high places, who are born from above and reckon themselves strangers here below; Calvin takes them for God's elect sons, who though dwellers on earth depend on heaven. Clarke doubts the received translation and would render it that the supreme holy ones shall receive the kingdom. On the everlasting possession Calvin raises a difficulty: the words seem to promise a perpetual condition, whereas counting the years of these monarchies gives nothing long enough to deserve the epithet. His answer is that the expression is measured by the feelings of the pious, to whom the delay seemed tedious beyond reckoning; and he turns it on his readers, asking what constancy would be found in us if the Church were oppressed a hundred years, when three or four months do not pass before men expostulate with God for not hastening to help.
19:
One detail in the repetition was not in the vision. Clarke points out that the brazen nails are not mentioned where the beast was first described, and reports that one scholar thought the words had dropped out of the earlier verse, though no manuscript intimates such a loss. Ellicott marks the claws as the new feature; Calvin reads the addition as meaning the beast would not merely attack all things but tear and devour them.

Why this beast alone drew the question is answered in the same terms by two of them. Gill says the prophet understood the first three well enough and wanted a particular account of the fourth because it threatened trouble to the church. Calvin finds the subjugation of so many kings the difference worth noticing: a few robbers seized a desert spot and grew great by brutal audacity until they had reduced all their neighbours, and at length were masters round the whole circuit of the Mediterranean, with no corner that did not receive their yoke.

Calvin reads the horns against Roman institutions. The ten horns he takes for provinces, a finite number standing for an indefinite one, and finds in them the difference from the other monarchies, since there never was one supreme ruler at Rome except briefly. The little horn he takes for the Caesars, who drew the whole government to themselves after depriving the people of their liberty and the senate of its power. The human eyes he explains by their cunning rather than open violence: they pretended to be tribunes of the people, left the ensigns of empire with the consuls, and on entering the senate sat low down in the seats prepared for tribunes; and though they professed the consular power supreme, they could not restrain their reproachful speeches.

Who makes war on the saints is the sharpest disagreement here. Gill rejects Antiochus, the Roman Caesars, and a Jewish identification with the conqueror of Jerusalem, and takes the horn for the pope of Rome, referring the war to the campaigns against the Waldenses. Clarke states the division evenly, that those who make Antiochus the little horn make the saints the Jewish people, while those who understand the popedom refer the words to the persecutions of the Waldenses and Albigenses. Calvin argues against the first at length. He grants the opinion is plausible, since Antiochus was hostile to the Jews beyond all others, and since the three years and a half in which the Temple lay in ruins answer to the time and times and half a time; but weighing all things shows how unsuitable it is. His objection is that Antiochus was not singular: he made war on the Church, and so did many others, the Egyptians having often spoiled the Temple and the Romans before the Caesars. The clause is comparative, and no war was carried on so continuously against the Church as those which followed the rise of the Caesars.

What the saints receive is defined carefully. Keil and Delitzsch rejects the rendering that the function of judging is given to the saints, as against a context in which God himself executes the judgment; what is given is justice procured by that judgment, the people of God being delivered from the beast and receiving the kingdom. Gill says the coming of the Ancient of days is not local, since he is omnipresent, but providential, to put a stop to the prevalence of the horn. Calvin explains the figure the same way, that God is said to sleep when he does not show himself as our deliverer and to come when he proves his care of us; and he dates the coming to the period after the promulgation of the gospel, when God lifted the Church out of the abyss. Ellicott adds that the war corresponds to the mouth speaking great things, and falls while the saints are expecting deliverance.
23:
How wide the fourth kingdom reached is measured against the others. Keil and Delitzsch reads the whole earth as the inhabited world, no hyperbole but the whole circle of the historical nations. Calvin makes the comparison from the other side: no state before had been so extensive, since the Spartans and Athenians were shut within narrow boundaries, and the wordy vanity of the Greeks led them to celebrate wars scarcely of any consequence.

What Calvin finds distinctive is the constitution rather than the extent. The empire had no single head; the senate held the chief authority while all power was centred in the people, so that the government was never settled. It was neither a republic nor a kingdom, he says, but a confused compound, in which the people exercised great power tumultuously and the senate oppressed them as much as it could. On that reckoning he denies that the ten horns mean kings succeeding one another in order, taking them for the multiform nature of a kingdom carried under more heads than one, the number standing for an indefinite plurality.

Others hold the horns contemporary but explain them otherwise. Keil and Delitzsch argues that since the ten horns stand together on one head the kings must be contemporary, so that what is symbolised is the dismemberment of the kingdom into ten principalities; Gill takes them for the kingdoms into which the empire was divided at its dissolution. Ellicott declines to choose: of the various attempts to account for the ten none have proved satisfactory, and we must wait in patient humility for the fulfilment, noting the marks by which the little horn may be identified.

Calvin holds to the Caesars and fits the three uprooted horns to them: after long strife the whole power passed to a conspiracy of three, and when discord followed, one was stripped of his place and lived on as if half dead, his life spared only because he had been raised to the chief priesthood. Wesley says instead that the horn seems to mean the Roman antichrist.

The great words are read as a claim to divinity. Gill renders the phrase at the side of the Most High, of one setting himself up as a rival; Keil and Delitzsch says the preposition denotes language by which he would set God aside and give himself out as God; Calvin takes the same construction and makes the pride of a king who ruled by hidden deceit consist in sitting as it were at God's side and against him. But Calvin denies that words here means doctrine. Those who understand the passage of Antichrist find their opinion confirmed by other tyrants having warred with arms rather than speech, but the prophet is not speaking so subtly: what is meant is the verbal boasting by which the Caesars promulgated edicts through the world, urging the proconsuls to punish the Christians. Clarke passes on the rendering of Symmachus, that he shall speak as if he were God, and applies the description to the popes of Rome, referring the wearing out of the saints to the persecution of those who refused their worship.

The marks and the measure of time close the answer. Ellicott lists three marks of identification, blasphemy of God, persecution of the saints, and attempts against all institutions of divine or human authority which appear ineffectual, since the horn only thinks to change them. On the period he reports that it is frequently explained as three years and a half, and sets out the assumptions that reading requires, that the plural stands for a dual and a time means a year, the total being taken either literally or as half a sabbatical period. Wesley says the numbers of Daniel and of John seem to agree.
26:
The sitting of the court is described only by its effect. Gill has the Judge take the bench with all prepared for arraignment and trial. Keil and Delitzsch notes that the judgment is set out solely in its consequences for the world-power, the destruction of the beast being passed over because it was mentioned already, while the taking away of its dominion is strengthened by two further infinitives; Ellicott notes the same omission. Calvin explains the phrase as before, that when all things proceed without punishment God is supposed to be at ease in heaven, and that in opposition to this he is said to ascend a tribunal whenever we feel his care over us.

When the beast died is Calvin's own question. When the Caesars transferred the empire to themselves the strength of the senate and people was enervated, but since the name remained the beast is not said to be slain until foreigners had become masters of Rome. Had the Romans been conquered a hundred times by professed enemies, he says, they would not have suffered such disgrace as when low-born men exercised a barbarous tyranny over them. So the angel marks the time correctly: it fell when foreigners unknown even in their own countries were raised beyond expectation to the highest honours, beheaded the noblest senators and put the meanest of men in their places by way of insult.

The kingdom given to the saints is taken as widely as the words allow. Gill says that not only the dominion taken from the horn but that of all others throughout the earth is given to the people of God, so that the kingdoms of this world become Christ's. Clarke adds that whatever name they may be distinguished by among men, theirs is the Church which no lapse of time shall injure and no power destroy. Keil and Delitzsch notes that the kingdom is given under the reign of the Son of man, supplied from the earlier verse.

Calvin uses the verse to say what the whole chapter is for. Any discussion of the four monarchies would have been cold and useless, he says, unless there had been added God's peculiar care of his own Church, since his elect are of more consequence than all the kingdoms in the world; so that when everything seems carried away by the blind impulse of chance we ought to contemplate God as watching for his Church and tempering all storms to its safety. He then grants the difficulty: this does not seem accomplished yet, and for that reason almost all have treated the prophecy as relating to the final advent; but he holds that they pervert the prophet's intention, and answers from the way the prophets everywhere speak magnificently of Christ's kingdom.

The closing words are read as a deliberate stop. Calvin says the vision is declared concluded so that the faithful might look for nothing beyond it, since we know what an insane disease a vain curiosity is; God adapts his teaching to our capacity, while we remain volatile and insatiable, asking why this was not added and why he stops here. Keil and Delitzsch takes the matter to mean not merely the angel's interpretation but the whole revelation, and Wesley the same; Ellicott says the prophet comforted himself by keeping the angel's words in his heart.

The prophet's distress ends the chapter. Calvin says the note of terror was added lest the pious should think the vision a vanished spectre, God wishing to stamp the certainty of the prophecy on his heart; and that his saying he kept the matter assures us he was a faithful interpreter. Clarke turns the verse on himself, saying that in considering the evils which must come before such times arrive, he may say with Daniel that his cogitations trouble him, but that he keeps his conjectures in his own heart.
